title: Chromatic Numbers and Finite Subgraph Inheritance

problemStatement.formal: Let G be a graph with chromatic number ℵ₁. Is there, for every cardinal m, some graph G_m of chromatic number m such that every finite subgraph of G_m is a subgraph of G?
problemStatement.plain: Taylor's conjecture: If G has chromatic number ℵ₁, can we build graphs of any chromatic number using only finite subgraphs of G? Komjáth-Shelah showed this is independent of ZFC - it can fail in some models.

proven: Lean formalization of chromatic number for infinite graphs (Cardinal-valued)
Formal statement of Taylor's conjecture using cardinals
Generalized conjecture for arbitrary uncountable κ
Machine-checked de Bruijn–Erdős coloring theorem (compactness form) via Mathlib's nonempty_hom_of_forall_finite_subgraph_hom
Machine-checked contrapositive: a non-n-colorable graph has a finite non-n-colorable subgraph
Bridge lemmas matching the custom Cardinal-valued chromatic number to Mathlib's Colorable predicate (the defining cardinal infimum is attained because cardinals are well-ordered)

Original discrete intermediate-value theorem (exists_induce_chiN_eq): in a finite graph, every chromatic value 0..χ is realized exactly by an induced subgraph; proved by Finset induction via a one-vertex extension lemma (adding a vertex raises χ by at most one)

Fully machine-checked finite_case: for finite χ(G)=k, every m ≤ k is realized as the chromatic number of an induced subgraph of G, giving automatic finite-subgraph inheritance (the last sorry is now discharged)

insights: The problem connects finite combinatorics to infinite graph theory
Independence from ZFC means the answer depends on set-theoretic axioms
Komjáth-Shelah: In some models, χ(H) ≤ ℵ₂ for all H with G's finite subgraphs
The De Bruijn-Erdős theorem provides a compactness principle for finite chromatic numbers
The gap between finite and uncountable chromatic numbers is fundamental: finite χ is computable from finite subgraphs, but uncountable χ requires genuinely infinite combinatorics
